name: Money maxxing / career maxxing

lead: Money maxxing and career maxxing mean pursuing income and professional success as a route to status and attractiveness, especially for men who see their looks as fixed.

The chain: higher income and career standing give status and resources, which raise perceived desirability and also pay for grooming, clothes, skincare and procedures. Evolutionary-psychology research reports that mate preferences track status and resources, and one cited study found higher-salaried men rated more attractive. Research also links perceived attractiveness to employment outcomes.

paras: People pursue promotions, higher-paying skills, businesses or investing, then spend part of the gains on appearance. It runs alongside or instead of looks work and plays out over years.
No direct health risks. Outcomes vary by person and culture, and the research findings are correlational.

angle.text: Looksmaxxing and manosphere communities present income and career success as a route to attractiveness: status and resources raise desirability and also pay for appearance upgrades. Mate-preference research partly supports a link between status and desirability.

lead: Money maxxing and career maxxing are looksmaxxing-community terms for building income, wealth and professional standing, usually as a complement to improving appearance. Members present money as a way to pay for grooming, skincare, clothing and cosmetic procedures, and as an independent source of attractiveness.[1][2]

Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article describes a person's "sexual market value" as combining looks with perceived status and wealth, and notes that status or finances can be a way of out-competing others in social settings.[2] Research summarized in Wikipedia reports that women's mate preferences track status cues such as resources and dominance, and that perceived attractiveness can affect how people are judged for employment.[1]

The practice is described in community posts rather than in studies of the strategy itself. A forum post by a 16-year-old, for instance, describes shifting attention from looksmaxxing to making money once appearance goals were met.[3]
infobox: Looksmaxxing spaces; term coined on incel message boards in the 2010s and popularized on TikTok in the 2020s (looksmaxxing generally)[2]

paras: Status is the relative social value attributed to a person, and socioeconomic status is typically indexed by income, education and occupational prestige.[4] Reference works report that women's preferences for male partners track status cues such as resources and dominance, and that attractiveness affects hiring and social opportunities.[1] One finding cited on Wikipedia reports that men with a higher salary were perceived as more attractive to women, and another study found a positive correlation between facial symmetry and salary among American football quarterbacks.[1] Evolutionary psychologists describe prestige as an important component of male attractiveness alongside dominance.[5]

Forum members describe money maxxing as a way to afford grooming, procedures and clothing, and as an independent source of attractiveness. Others dispute how much money can offset looks.[3] Threads on the topic cover side jobs, investing and business ideas, and members ask whether starting college or a career later than peers matters. These are community positions, not research findings.
Wikipedia describes the community's "sexual market value" framework, in which looks combine with perceived status and wealth.[2]
No studies found. Economics and psychology literature on attractiveness and income exists but does not evaluate money maxxing as a practice.[1]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, money maxxing is discussed as a second track beside looks, with members trading income ideas and debating whether wealth can offset or amplify appearance.[3]
